newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Battle for Kabul rages despite U.N. truce call.
newsitem.headline: Battle for Kabul rages despite U.N. truce call.

text.p: Afghan government forces and the rebel Taleban militia fought on around the capital Kabul on Thursday, ignoring a U.N. Security Council call for an immediate ceasefire, Afghan sources in neighbouring Pakistan said.

A Taleban source in the northwest Pakistan town of Peshawar said the Islamic militia forces had penetrated eastern Kabul overnight and were only about five km (three miles) from the presidential palace.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) also quoted other Taleban sources as saying the militia had broken through government frontlines in the south and southwest of Kabul.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the reports.
Taleban fighters fired rockets at the city overnight, killing at least nine people and wounding 16, the AIP said.
It said fighting raged in the eastern suburbs of Kabul on Thursday morning after a comparative lull over night, with the Taleban holding positions it had captured on Wednesday.
A Taleban source in Peshawar denied a Kabul government report on Wednesday night that its forces had repulsed the militia from the east of the capital.

The source, speaking anonymously, said Taleban forces entered the city from Pul-i-Charkhi village, which they said they had captured on Wednesday in a swift advance after seizing the strategic eastern town of Sarobi.
Official Kabul Radio said on Wednesday night the Taleban had cut off electrictiy to Kabul only 10 days after it was restored to part of the city from an eastern power house after two years.
The appeal for a ceasefire was announced after a meeting of the 15-nation Security Council in New York.

"The members of the council call upon the parties to stop fighting immediately, to agree to a ceasefire and to enter into serious negotiations to find a political solution to this conflict," the current council president, Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau, told reporters.
The council, which has made similar appeals before without success, was particularly concerned by the humanitarian crisis and the risk of civilian casualties in the fighting for Kabul.
The Afghan government asked the Security Council to meet on the crisis and accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban.
Earlier, a top U.N. official had said the radical Islamic group could be on the verge of taking Kabul, as government resistance to its onslaught seeemed to be crumbling.
But Afghan Deputy Foreign Minister Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai told reporters in New York that the government had inflicted heavy casualties on the attackers and now wanted a ceasefire.
"The Taleban have been pushed back... They have sustained heavy casualties... Apparently, there is not any obvious danger to the security of Kabul," Ghafoorzai said.
Government forces had killed 150 fighters from the militant Islamic group, wounded 500 more and destroyed 18 tanks and 12 other vehicles in the Kabul fighting, he said.
Taleban controls more than half of Afghanistan, which has seen continuous fighting between Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops propping a communist government withdrew in 1989.

Emerging two years ago from the obscurity of religious schools in Pakistan, Taleban has been fighting to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
Pakistan's U.N. Ambassador, Ahmad Kamal, denied his country was involved in the conflict and said there was no serious fighting, because there was almost no resistance to the Taleban.

"What appears to be happening is that the Taleban is advancing...on the basis of what appear to be either defections or desertions," he told reporters. "Everybody is surprised at the manner in which the front is collapsing."
